options.text: It is prerendered at build time and served as static HTML
options.why: Prerendering is the default for anything that does not use request-time APIs or uncached data.

options.text: It is rendered on the server for every request, like any Server Component
options.why: Server Components are not dynamic by default; they run at build time unless something needs the request.

options.text: It is rendered only in the browser after the JavaScript bundle loads
options.why: Pages are Server Components and produce HTML on the server, not in the browser.

options.text: It is rendered on the first request and then never cached
options.why: That describes on-demand rendering of an unlisted dynamic param, not a static page.

explanation: In the App Router, components that do not use request-time APIs (cookies, headers, searchParams, draftMode) or uncached data are prerendered during `next build`. The route shows as `○ Static` in the build output and is served as HTML without server rendering on each request.

stem: On a client-side navigation to another route, Next.js fetches that route's server-rendered HTML and swaps it into the page.

options.text: True
options.why: Only the first load uses HTML. Client navigations fetch the RSC payload instead.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct: navigations fetch only the component payload (with an `rsc: 1` header), and Client Components render in the browser.

explanation: On the first load, the browser gets HTML for a fast preview, the RSC payload to reconcile the tree, and JavaScript to hydrate. On subsequent navigations, Next.js fetches (or reuses a prefetched) RSC payload and renders Client Components entirely on the client. No HTML is transferred.
reference: Next.js docs: Server and Client Components (Subsequent Navigations)

stem: Which special file, placed next to `page.tsx`, makes Next.js wrap the page in a `<Suspense>` boundary and show its UI instantly while the page streams in? Type the file name without the extension.
explanation: `loading.js` is nested inside the segment's `layout.js` and wraps `page.js` (and anything below it) in a `<Suspense>` boundary, using the loading component as the fallback. The fallback is also prefetched, so navigation to the segment feels immediate.

stem: In the App Router without Cache Components, which three of these, used in a page, opt it into dynamic (request-time) rendering? (Choose three.)

options.text: `await cookies()`
options.why: Cookies are only known per request, so the route must render at request time.

options.text: Reading the `searchParams` prop
options.why: Query strings are only known when the request arrives.

options.text: `await headers()`
options.why: Request headers are a request-time API like cookies.

options.text: Exporting `generateStaticParams`
options.why: It does the opposite: it lists params to prerender at build time.

options.text: Reading a config file with `fs.readFileSync`
options.why: Synchronous reads complete during prerendering and end up in the static HTML.

options.text: Rendering a Client Component that uses `useState`
options.why: Client Components are still prerendered to HTML; state does not make the route dynamic.

explanation: Request-time APIs (`cookies()`, `headers()`, `searchParams` and `draftMode()`) depend on the incoming request, so a page that uses them is rendered per request. Without Cache Components this opts the whole route into dynamic rendering. Client state and synchronous file reads do not.

stem: What is `generateStaticParams` used for in the App Router?

options.text: Listing the dynamic segment values to prerender at build time
options.why: Each returned object becomes one prerendered URL for the dynamic route.

options.text: Validating the search params before the page renders
options.why: It has nothing to do with search params; it fills dynamic segments like `[slug]`.

options.text: Declaring which route params a Client Component may read
options.why: Client Components read params with hooks; this function controls build-time generation.

options.text: Generating the `params` object for each request
options.why: It runs at build time (and on navigation in dev), not per request in production.

explanation: `generateStaticParams` returns an array like `[{ slug: 'a' }, { slug: 'b' }]`. During `next build`, Next.js prerenders one version of the page per entry. It replaces `getStaticPaths` from the Pages Router.

stem: Match each symbol in the `next build` route table with what it means.

options.text: Fully prerendered at build time; served without server rendering
Static shell served immediately; dynamic parts stream at request time
Prerendered HTML generated from generateStaticParams
Server-rendered on demand for each request

explanation: `○` Static, `●` SSG and `ƒ` Dynamic are the classic modes. Cache Components adds `◐` Partial Prerender, where each route has a static shell plus dynamic parts that stream in. With Cache Components a route shows `ƒ` only when there is nothing to prerender, such as request-dependent Route Handlers.

stem: Working without Cache Components, `app/blog/[slug]/page.tsx` exports `dynamicParams = false`, and its `generateStaticParams` returns the slugs `a` and `b`. What happens when someone visits `/blog/c`?

options.text: It returns a 404 page, since only listed params are served
options.why: `dynamicParams = false` limits the route to the params returned at build time.

options.text: It renders `c` on demand at request time and caches the result
options.why: That is the default (`dynamicParams = true`) behaviour, which this route turned off.

options.text: The request fails with a 500 error because `c` was never built
options.why: Unknown params are not treated as server errors; they are not-found.

options.text: It redirects to `/blog/a`, the first param that was listed
options.why: Next.js never redirects to another param on its own.

explanation: With `dynamicParams = true` (the default), params missing from `generateStaticParams` are generated at request time. With `false`, they return a 404. This replaces `fallback: false` from `getStaticPaths`. Note that Cache Components does not support `dynamicParams` at all.

stem: A page awaits a 3-second database query in its top-level component before returning any JSX. You move the query into a child component and wrap that child in `<Suspense>` with a skeleton fallback. What changes most for the user?

options.text: TTFB and first paint stop waiting for the query; the skeleton shows at once
options.why: The shell and fallback stream immediately, and the query result streams in later.

options.text: The query itself finishes faster, because Suspense runs it in parallel with rendering
options.why: Suspense does not speed up the query; it only stops it from blocking the rest of the page.

options.text: Nothing changes, because streamed HTML stays invisible until hydration finishes
options.why: Streamed HTML paints as it arrives, before JavaScript loads or hydration runs.

options.text: The page now renders in the browser instead of on the server
options.why: Both versions render on the server; only the delivery is progressive.

explanation: Without streaming, TTFB equals the slowest query, because the server waits for all data before sending HTML. With a `<Suspense>` boundary, the server sends the static shell (layouts, headings, fallbacks) as soon as it is ready, so TTFB and FCP no longer depend on the data.

stem: Working without Cache Components, a product page renders a static `<Header />`, a `<Products />` list fetched with `cache: 'force-cache'`, and deep in the tree a `<Greeting />` that reads `(await cookies()).get('name')`. How is the route rendered?

options.text: The entire route becomes dynamic: one cookies() call makes it render per request
options.why: In the previous model, using a request-time API anywhere opts the whole route into dynamic rendering.

options.text: Header and Products are prerendered into a shell, and only Greeting renders per request
options.why: That component-level split is what Cache Components adds; the previous model is route-level.

options.text: It is prerendered, and cookies() just returns an empty store at build time
options.why: Empty cookies only happen when the route is forced static with `dynamic = 'force-static'`.

options.text: The build fails until cookies() is wrapped in a Suspense boundary in Next 16
options.why: That build error is a Cache Components validation, which this project does not use.

explanation: Without Cache Components, static versus dynamic is decided per route. A single request-time API, here `cookies()`, opts the route into dynamic rendering, so it shows as `ƒ` and renders on every request. The cached fetch still serves from the data cache, but the HTML is produced per request.
reference: Next.js docs: Caching (Static, cached, and streaming)

stem:
Now the same project sets `cacheComponents: true`, and `` (which reads `cookies()`) is wrapped in `Hi there

}>`. What does the build report, and what does a visitor receive?

options.text: `◐`: a static shell with the fallback is served, and Greeting streams in per request
options.why: Only the Suspense subtree waits for the request; everything else is prerendered.

options.text: `ƒ`: the cookies() call still makes the entire route render dynamically on every request
options.why: With Cache Components, a runtime API inside Suspense no longer opts the whole route out.

options.text: `○`: the page is fully static and cookies() reads the build machine's cookies
options.why: Cookies are never read at build time; that part is deferred to request time.

options.text: `●`: one HTML file is generated for each cookie value seen during the build
options.why: Static generation is driven by route params, never by cookie values.

explanation: Cache Components makes Partial Prerendering the default. At build time, Next.js renders the tree; the Suspense fallback goes into the static shell while the component that reads cookies streams at request time. The docs stress that reading `cookies()` here does not opt the whole route into dynamic rendering the way the previous model did.
reference: Next.js docs: Caching (Working with runtime APIs)

stem: `app/blog/page.tsx` exports `revalidate = 60` (no Cache Components). It was built at 12:00:00 and nobody visits until 12:05:00. What does that first visitor at 12:05 receive?

options.text: The 12:00 page, while a fresh version regenerates in the background
options.why: ISR is stale-while-revalidate: the stale page is served and regeneration starts.

options.text: A freshly rendered page, because the cached copy expired four minutes ago
options.why: Expiry does not block the visitor; they get the stale copy instantly.

options.text: A 503 response until the regeneration finishes, then the new page
options.why: Next.js never makes visitors wait on regeneration with an error.

options.text: The cached page, which only regenerates after a call to revalidatePath
options.why: Time-based revalidation needs no explicit call; the request itself triggers it.

explanation: After the revalidate window passes, the next request still gets the cached (stale) page immediately. That request triggers a background regeneration, and once it succeeds the new version replaces the cached one for later visitors.

stem: A page uses `export const revalidate = 60`. Put these events in order, starting from the build.

options.text: `next build` prerenders the page and caches it
Requests within the next 60 seconds get the cached page instantly
After 60 seconds, the next request still gets the cached, now stale, page
That request triggers a background regeneration of the page
Once regeneration succeeds, later requests get the new page

explanation: This is the ISR cycle from the docs: prerender at build, serve from cache while fresh, serve stale after the window while regenerating in the background, then serve the new version. If regeneration fails, the last good page keeps being served.

stem: Working without Cache Components, a page exports `dynamic = 'force-static'` and renders `(await cookies()).get('theme')?.value ?? 'light'`. What theme does each visitor see?

options.text: `light` for everyone: force-static makes cookies() return empty values
options.why: Forcing static rendering stubs out request-time APIs instead of failing.

options.text: Their own theme, because cookies() overrides force-static at request time
options.why: force-static wins: the route is prerendered, so there is no request to read.

options.text: None: the build fails with an error about using cookies() in a static route
options.why: Failing on request-time APIs is what `dynamic = 'error'` does, not force-static.

options.text: `light` on the first visit, then their own theme after the next revalidation
options.why: Revalidation re-renders statically too, so cookies stay empty.

explanation: In the previous model, `force-static` forces prerendering by making `cookies()`, `headers()` and `useSearchParams()` return empty values. The page can still be revalidated with `revalidate`, `revalidatePath` or `revalidateTag`. Use `dynamic = 'error'` if you want the build to fail instead.

stem:
A page renders this Client Component: ```tsx 'use client' export default function Hello() { console.log('Hello rendered') return

Hello

} ``` Where does `Hello rendered` appear on a direct visit to the page, and where on a later client-side navigation to it?

options.text: Direct visit: only the browser console. Navigation: only the browser console
options.why: On a direct visit the Client Component is also server-rendered to HTML, so the log appears in the terminal too.

options.text: Direct visit: only the server terminal. Navigation: only the server terminal
options.why: A Client Component also hydrates and re-renders in the browser, so its log reaches the browser console.

options.text: Direct visit: terminal and browser console. Navigation: only the browser console
options.why: It renders on the server for the HTML, then in the browser to hydrate; a navigation renders it in the browser only.

options.text: Direct visit: terminal and browser console. Navigation: terminal and console again
options.why: On a client-side navigation the server sends the RSC Payload, and the Client Component renders only in the browser.

explanation: "Client Component" means the code also runs in the browser, not that it runs only there. On a direct visit Next.js renders the Client Component on the server to produce HTML (log in the terminal) and React renders it again in the browser during hydration (log in the console). On a client-side navigation the server returns the RSC Payload without HTML for that component, so it renders only in the browser. Server Components, by contrast, never run in the browser.
reference: Next.js docs: Server and Client Boundary (Rendering environments)

stem: With Cache Components, wrapping a component in `<Suspense>` is enough to make it render at request time, even if it only does synchronous work.

options.text: True
options.why: Suspense only provides a fallback; it never opts anything into dynamic rendering.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct: synchronous work completes during prerendering, Suspense or not.

explanation: The docs state that `<Suspense>` provides fallback UI while async work completes but does not itself opt a component into dynamic rendering. A component that only does synchronous work finishes during prerendering and lands in the static shell. To defer work to request time, await `connection()` or a runtime API.

stem: `app/dashboard/` contains `layout.tsx`, `template.tsx`, `loading.tsx`, `error.tsx`, `not-found.tsx` and `page.tsx`, plus a nested `settings/layout.tsx`. Which three does the `<Suspense>` boundary from `dashboard/loading.tsx` wrap? (Choose three.)

options.text: `dashboard/page.tsx`
options.why: loading.js wraps the page in its own segment.

options.text: `dashboard/not-found.tsx`
options.why: The not-found UI sits inside the loading boundary in the component hierarchy.

options.text: `dashboard/settings/layout.tsx`
options.why: Nested layouts below the segment are inside the boundary too.

options.text: `dashboard/layout.tsx`
options.why: loading.js is nested inside the same-segment layout, so it cannot wrap it.

options.text: `dashboard/error.tsx`
options.why: The error boundary sits outside loading in the same segment.

options.text: `dashboard/template.tsx`
options.why: The template also wraps loading, not the other way round.

explanation: In the component hierarchy, `loading.js` wraps `not-found.js`, `page.js` and nested `layout.js` files in a `<Suspense>` boundary. It does not wrap the `layout.js`, `template.js` or `error.js` of the same segment. That is why a slow layout is not covered by its own loading UI.

stem: With Cache Components, a component renders `crypto.randomUUID()` and must show a new value on every request. Type the name of the function from `next/server` that you `await` first (and then wrap the component in `<Suspense>`).
explanation: `await connection()` tells Next.js to wait for an incoming request before continuing, so prerendering stops there. It is the documented fix for `Math.random()`, `Date.now()` and `crypto.randomUUID()` when you want a unique value per request. The alternative is `'use cache'`, which shares one value across users.

stem: Working without Cache Components, `app/blog/[slug]/page.tsx` should prerender no slugs at build time but statically render each one on its first visit. Which two setups do that? (Choose two.)

options.text: `generateStaticParams` returns an empty array `[]`
options.why: An empty list means nothing at build time, with each path statically rendered on first visit.

options.text: The page exports `dynamic = 'force-static'`
options.why: The docs list force-static as the other way to render all paths at runtime statically.

options.text: `generateStaticParams` is defined but returns nothing (`undefined`)
options.why: You must return an array; otherwise the route is dynamically rendered.

options.text: The page exports `dynamicParams = false`
options.why: That makes every unlisted slug, here all of them, return 404.

options.text: The page exports `revalidate = 0`
options.why: That forces dynamic rendering on every request, the opposite of static.

explanation: To statically render all paths the first time they are visited, return `[]` from `generateStaticParams` or export `dynamic = 'force-static'`. Not returning an array makes the route dynamic. With Cache Components the rules change: `[]` becomes a build error.
reference: Next.js docs: generateStaticParams (All paths at runtime)

stem: A product page renders `<Suspense fallback={<Skeleton />}><Product id={id} /></Suspense>`, and `Product` calls `notFound()` after its fetch finds nothing. What does a crawler receive for a missing product?

options.text: HTTP 200 with the not-found UI and a `noindex` robots meta tag
options.why: The status was sent with the shell, so Next.js marks the page noindex instead.

options.text: HTTP 404, because notFound() always sets the response status code
options.why: It can only set 404 if it runs before the response starts streaming.

options.text: HTTP 500, since an error was thrown after the response had begun
options.why: notFound() is handled as not-found UI, not as a server error.

options.text: HTTP 302 redirecting the crawler to the app's `/404` route
options.why: Next.js renders not-found UI in place; it does not redirect.

explanation: Streaming commits to `200 OK` when the first chunk (here, the Suspense fallback) is sent. If `notFound()` fires mid-stream, Next.js cannot change the status, so it injects `<meta name="robots" content="noindex">` into the streamed HTML so search engines do not index the page.

stem: With `cacheComponents: true`, match each piece of a page with how Next.js handles it at build time.

options.text: Its rendered output is included in the static shell
Its fallback is in the shell; the content streams at request time
Prerendering fails with a validation error until it is handled
Prerendered to HTML in the shell, then hydrated in the browser

prompts.text: An async component with `'use cache'` and `cacheLife('hours')`
A component that renders `Math.random()` with no `connection()` and no `'use cache'`

explanation: During prerendering, cached results with a long enough lifetime join the static shell. Runtime API access inside Suspense contributes only its fallback. Random values and timestamps must be handled explicitly with `connection()` or `'use cache'`, or the dev overlay and build report them. Client Components are still prerendered to HTML and hydrated later.

options.text: Do a fast existence check in the page and call notFound() before the Suspense boundary
options.why: Before anything suspends, no headers have been sent, so a real 404 is still possible.

options.text: Move the notFound() call into the Skeleton fallback so it runs before streaming starts
options.why: The fallback is itself the first streamed chunk, which commits the 200 status.

options.text: Export `dynamic = 'force-dynamic'` so the status code can be decided per request instead
options.why: Rendering per request does not help; the status is still sent when streaming begins.

options.text: Throw `new Response(null, { status: 404 })` from inside Product while it renders
options.why: Throwing a Response from a component is not how Next.js sets status codes.

explanation: The body starts streaming when a Suspense fallback renders or a component suspends. To get a real status code, call `notFound()` before any `await` that may suspend and before any `<Suspense>` boundary, for example after a fast existence check. You can also reject missing slugs earlier in Proxy.
reference: Next.js docs: Streaming (When does streaming start?)

stem: Inside a `<Suspense>` boundary, a component awaits a slow fetch and then calls `redirect('/login')` because the session has expired. The page's shell has already been sent. What happens?

options.text: It becomes a client-side redirect, since the status and headers were already sent
options.why: Mid-stream, Next.js cannot send a 3xx, so the browser navigates instead.

options.text: Next.js discards the streamed HTML and replies with a 307 Location header instead
options.why: Once the first chunk is out, the response status can no longer change.

options.text: Nothing: redirect() is ignored once streaming starts
options.why: It is not ignored; it is delivered through the stream as a client-side redirect.

options.text: A trailing 307 header is appended so the browser follows it after the stream ends
options.why: HTTP has no way to add a status code after the body has started.

explanation: Once streaming begins, the status code and headers are fixed. A `redirect()` thrown mid-stream is therefore handled in the streamed HTML as a client-side redirect rather than an HTTP redirect header. For a real 307 or 308, redirect before anything suspends, in Proxy, or with `next.config.js` redirects.

stem: A dashboard streams three sections, each in its own `<Suspense>`. After the shell is sent, the Revenue section throws an error during rendering. Which two statements are true? (Choose two.)

options.text: The response status stays 200, because it was sent with the first chunk
options.why: Status codes cannot change after streaming starts.

options.text: The nearest error boundary renders its error UI in place of what failed
options.why: The error is handled inside the streamed HTML by the closest error.js boundary.

options.text: The server switches the status to 500 and restarts the stream from scratch
options.why: The status is already committed, and Next.js does not restart responses.

options.text: The browser receives a blank page because the whole stream is aborted
options.why: The error is contained by a boundary instead of tearing down the response.

options.text: Next.js keeps retrying the render on the server until Revenue succeeds
options.why: There is no automatic retry loop for render errors.

explanation: If a component throws after streaming has started, the nearest `error.js` boundary catches it and renders the error UI in its place. Because `200 OK` was sent with the first chunk, the status cannot become 4xx or 5xx, so the error is handled entirely within the streamed HTML.

options.text: The layout can't prerender; await the params promise inside a Suspense child instead
options.why: An unknown param is runtime data, so awaiting it at the top blocks the layout's shell.

options.text: There is no problem: params are known once the request arrives, so the shell is complete
options.why: The shell is built before any request, when unlisted params are still unknown.

options.text: Only the page loses its shell, because layouts are always prerendered regardless of params
options.why: Layouts follow the same rules; awaiting runtime data blocks them too.

options.text: Add `'use cache'` to the layout so the awaited params can be resolved during the build
options.why: Caching cannot make an unknown param known at build time.

explanation: If a param is not provided by `generateStaticParams`, it is runtime data, and a layout that awaits it at the top cannot be prerendered. Keep the layout non-async and resolve `params` inside a `<Suspense>` boundary (for example `params.then(({ slug }) => <SlugHeading slug={slug} />)`). Then `<Sidebar />`, `{children}` and the fallback join the static shell.
reference: Next.js docs: Caching (Maximizing the static shell)

stem: With Cache Components, `generateStaticParams` for `/docs/[slug]` returns `[]` because the slugs come from a CMS at runtime. What happens at `next build`?

options.text: The build fails: with Cache Components it must return at least one param
options.why: An empty array is rejected so Next.js can validate the route's runtime access.

options.text: Nothing is prerendered, and each slug is statically rendered on its first visit
options.why: That is the previous model's behaviour for `[]`, not the Cache Components one.

options.text: Every slug renders dynamically on each request, with no static shell at all
options.why: Routes always get a shell under Cache Components; here the build stops earlier.

options.text: The route is skipped by the build and all of its URLs return 404
options.why: Next.js does not silently skip routes; it reports the empty list.

explanation: With Cache Components, `generateStaticParams` must return at least one param, or the build fails with the empty-generate-static-params error. That lets Cache Components check that the route does not wrongly access `cookies()`, `headers()` or `searchParams`. A placeholder param handled with `notFound()` is a documented workaround, at the cost of weaker validation.

stem: Working without Cache Components, `app/news/page.tsx` exports `revalidate = 300`. Which two `fetch` calls in that route would make it render dynamically on every request instead of using ISR? (Choose two.)

options.text: `fetch(url, { cache: 'no-store' })`
options.why: An explicit no-store fetch makes the route dynamic.

options.text: `fetch(url, { next: { revalidate: 0 } })`
options.why: A revalidate time of 0 also forces dynamic rendering.

options.text: `fetch(url, { next: { revalidate: 3600 } })`
options.why: A positive revalidate keeps ISR; only the shortest window matters.

options.text: `fetch(url, { cache: 'force-cache' })`
options.why: Forcing the cache is compatible with ISR.

options.text: `fetch(url, { next: { tags: ['news'] } })`
options.why: Tags only enable on-demand invalidation; they do not opt out of caching.

explanation: From the ISR caveats: if any `fetch` in a route has a `revalidate` of `0` or an explicit `no-store`, the route is dynamically rendered. Other positive revalidate values only affect how often the route regenerates, with the lowest one winning.

stem: Working without Cache Components, a route's layout exports `revalidate = 300`, its page exports `revalidate = 3600`, and the page also calls `fetch(url, { next: { revalidate: 120 } })`. Every how many seconds can ISR regenerate the route? Type a number.
explanation: The lowest `revalidate` across a route's layouts and pages sets the route's frequency (300 here). An individual `fetch` can set an even lower value, which raises the frequency of the whole route, and with several fetches the lowest is used. So the route can regenerate every 120 seconds.
reference: Next.js docs: Caching (Previous Model), Revalidation frequency

stem: An ISR page (`revalidate = 600`) starts regenerating in the background, but the CMS is down and the render throws. What do visitors get?

options.text: The last successfully generated page, retried on a later request
options.why: A failed regeneration never replaces the good cached version.

options.text: The error page, until the CMS recovers and someone redeploys the site
options.why: Visitors keep getting the cached page; no redeploy is needed.

options.text: An empty shell, because the failed render replaced the cached page
options.why: The cache is only updated after a successful regeneration.

options.text: A 500 for exactly 600 seconds, and then the old page again
options.why: Errors are not cached for the revalidate window.

explanation: If an error is thrown while revalidating, the last successfully generated data keeps being served from the cache, and Next.js retries on the next request. Regeneration failures are therefore invisible to users, which is why monitoring the logs matters.
reference: Next.js docs: Incremental Static Regeneration (Handling uncaught exceptions)

stem: While self-hosting an ISR route, you inspect the `x-nextjs-cache` response header. Match each value with what it means.

options.text: Served from the cache, still fresh
Served from the cache while it regenerates in the background
Not in the cache; rendered fresh for this request
Regenerated through on-demand revalidation

explanation: The `x-nextjs-cache` header shows ISR at work: `HIT` (fresh from cache), `STALE` (served from cache while regenerating), `MISS` (not cached, rendered now) and `REVALIDATED` (regenerated by on-demand revalidation). Watching it for `STALE` then `HIT` is the quickest way to confirm a revalidate window works.

stem: A Client Component renders `new Date(event.date).toLocaleDateString()`. The server runs with `LANG=ja_JP.UTF-8`, and users browse in other locales, so React reports a hydration error. Which approach from the Next.js guide shows the user's format before first paint, with no hydration error?

options.text: An inline script rewrites the text before paint, plus suppressHydrationWarning
options.why: The script fixes the DOM during parsing, and the flag tells React to keep the DOM.

options.text: Set the formatted date in useEffect after mount so the server and first client render match
options.why: This avoids the error, but users first see the server format and then a flash.

options.text: Turn it into a Server Component, so the date is formatted once on the server for everyone
options.why: There is no error, but the date is then permanently in the server's locale.

options.text: Add suppressHydrationWarning to the element so that React keeps the client's formatted value
options.why: With the flag, the DOM wins, so the server's format stays on screen.

explanation: The guide renders the server value, places a synchronous inline `<script>` after the element that rewrites `textContent` with the browser's locale before first paint, and adds `suppressHydrationWarning` so React accepts the corrected DOM. The `useEffect` approach flashes, and a Server Component freezes the server's locale.
reference: Next.js docs: Preventing flash before hydration

stem: A page has two sibling `<Suspense>` boundaries: Weather resolves after 1 second and Analytics after 3 seconds. Put the chunks of the streamed HTML response in the order they arrive.

options.text: The static shell: head, CSS, layout and both fallbacks with `<template>` placeholders
The component payload (`self.__next_f.push`) used for hydration
Weather's HTML in a hidden div, plus a script that swaps it into its placeholder
Analytics' HTML and its swap script

explanation: The docs' stream observer shows chunk 0 as the static shell with `<template id="B:0">` placeholders and bootstrap scripts, then the component payload, then each boundary's content (`<div hidden id="S:0">` plus a swap script) as it resolves. Sibling boundaries stream independently, so the faster one arrives first.
reference: Next.js docs: Streaming (Verifying that streaming works)

stem: During ISR background revalidation of `/blog/[slug]`, Next.js calls `generateStaticParams` again to discover newly published slugs.

options.text: True
options.why: `generateStaticParams` runs at build time (and on navigation in dev), not during revalidation.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct: the docs say it is not called again during revalidation.

explanation: During `next build`, `generateStaticParams` runs before the pages are generated. During ISR it is not called again, so new slugs are handled by `dynamicParams` (rendered on first visit by default) rather than by re-running the function.

stem: Every page shows an "Exit preview" `<Link href="/api/draft/disable">` that points at a `GET` Route Handler calling `(await draftMode()).disable()`. Editors report that preview switches itself off right after they enable it. Why?

options.text: The Link's prefetch calls the GET handler, which clears the bypass cookie
options.why: Links are prefetched by default, so the exit route runs before anyone clicks.

options.text: draftMode() lasts for one request only, unless enable() is called again on every page
options.why: The `__prerender_bypass` cookie persists until something disables it.

options.text: Draft Mode only works on routes that also export `dynamic = 'force-dynamic'`
options.why: Draft Mode works on static, cached and ISR pages alike.

options.text: Route Handlers cannot set or delete cookies, so the draft cookie never sticks
options.why: Route Handlers are exactly where enable() and disable() are called.

explanation: `draft.enable()` sets the `__prerender_bypass` cookie and `disable()` deletes it. Because `<Link>` prefetches by default, a link to a `GET` exit handler fires on prefetch and clears the cookie. Use a Server Action or `POST` handler for exiting, or at least `prefetch={false}`. Forms are never prefetched.

stem: A Server Component page imports a heavy `'use client'` chart with `const Chart = dynamic(() => import('./chart'))`, expecting its JavaScript to be split out and loaded on demand. What do the Next.js docs say about this?

options.text: Automatic code splitting isn't supported for a Client Component imported this way
options.why: Move the dynamic() call into a Client Component to get a lazy-loaded chunk.

options.text: It works as intended: the chart gets its own chunk, loaded only when it first renders
options.why: That holds when the dynamic import lives in a Client Component, not here.

options.text: It throws, because next/dynamic cannot be imported into Server Components at all
options.why: next/dynamic is allowed in Server Components; only `ssr: false` is rejected there.

options.text: It works, but only if `ssr: false` is also passed so the server skips the chart
options.why: `ssr: false` errors in Server Components, so this would make things worse.

explanation: The lazy-loading guide notes that when a Server Component dynamically imports a Client Component, automatic code splitting is currently not supported. Dynamically importing a Server Component lazy-loads only its Client Component children. For true on-demand loading, call `next/dynamic` (or `React.lazy`) from inside a Client Component.

stem: One `<Suspense>` boundary contains two dates, each corrected by an inline script before first paint. One element has `suppressHydrationWarning`; on the other it was forgotten. What happens during hydration?

options.text: React treats it as an error and client-renders the boundary, losing both script fixes
options.why: The unmarked mismatch triggers recovery, which rebuilds the boundary's DOM.

options.text: Only the unmarked date flashes back to the server format; the marked one keeps its fix
options.why: Recovery rebuilds the whole boundary, so the marked element's fix is lost too.

options.text: Both keep their corrected text, since one flag covers the entire boundary
options.why: suppressHydrationWarning applies to a single element only.

options.text: React quietly patches only the unmarked text node and logs a warning
options.why: A text mismatch without the flag is an error that forces client rendering.

explanation: Without `suppressHydrationWarning`, React treats a text mismatch as a hydration error and recovers by client-rendering from the nearest error or Suspense boundary. Inline-script corrections on other elements in that boundary are lost, because the scripts do not re-run when React rebuilds the DOM. Every corrected element needs the flag.
reference: Next.js docs: Preventing flash before hydration (suppressHydrationWarning)

stem: Streaming works with `next start` on your laptop, but in production the whole page appears at once, after the slowest query. Which two are likely causes? (Choose two.)

options.text: An Nginx reverse proxy buffering the response (fix: `X-Accel-Buffering: no`)
options.why: Nginx buffers by default, so chunks only reach the browser at the end.

options.text: AWS Lambda running without response streaming mode enabled
options.why: Lambda only streams when that mode is explicitly turned on.

options.text: Having too many Suspense boundaries on the page
options.why: More boundaries mean more streaming points, not fewer.

options.text: Using Server Components rather than Client Components
options.why: Server Components are what stream; this would not buffer anything.

options.text: Not exporting `dynamic = 'force-dynamic'` from the page
options.why: Streaming does not depend on that segment config.

explanation: Any layer that buffers the response defeats streaming. The docs call out reverse proxies such as Nginx (disable with `X-Accel-Buffering: no`), CDNs that buffer, serverless platforms such as AWS Lambda without response streaming mode, and compression layers that flush too rarely.
reference: Next.js docs: Streaming (What can affect streaming)

stem: With Cache Components, a page's static shell reads a JSON file that only exists on the build machine; it is not deployed. Real users see the page fine, but link previews from Twitterbot fail to render. Why?

options.text: HTML-limited bots get a full request-time render, where the file doesn't exist
options.why: Crawlers get a fresh full render so metadata lands in the head.

options.text: Bots receive only the Suspense fallbacks, and those fallbacks reference the missing file
options.why: Bots get a complete document, not the fallbacks.

options.text: Twitterbot cannot run JavaScript, so it never receives the shell's HTML
options.why: The shell is HTML; the issue is that it is re-rendered for the bot.

options.text: Bots are served the App Shell from a separate cache that was not deployed
options.why: There is no separate bot cache; the bot triggers a request-time render.

explanation: Visitors and DOM-capable crawlers get the prerendered shell without re-running its code. HTML-limited bots are detected by user agent and get the whole page rendered dynamically at request time, so `generateMetadata` can fill the `<head>`. Any shell input that only existed at build time then fails. The docs warn to make shell data available at request time too.

stem: After enabling Cache Components, a page fails to build with a blocking-prerender-random error from `Math.random()` in render. A teammate adds `export const instant = false` to the page. What happens?

options.text: It still fails: instant = false doesn't clear synchronous IO errors
options.why: It only marks the segment as allowed to block; random values still need handling.

options.text: The build passes and the page becomes dynamic (`ƒ`)
options.why: `instant = false` never forces a route dynamic.

options.text: The build passes, and Math.random() simply runs once per request
options.why: Per-request values need `connection()` plus Suspense, not this flag.

options.text: The build passes, and one Math.random() value is baked into the shell
options.why: Sharing a value across users needs `'use cache'`, not instant = false.

explanation: `instant = false` defers navigation-blocking validation for a segment. It does not make the route dynamic, and it does not clear synchronous IO build errors from `new Date()`, `Date.now()`, `Math.random()` or `crypto.randomUUID()`. Fix those with `await connection()` inside `<Suspense>`, `'use cache'`, or by moving the call into a Client Component.
reference: Next.js docs: Migrating to Cache Components (Opting out of validation)

stem: A page in a Next.js 16 app still exports `runtime = 'edge'`. Which two statements are true? (Choose two.)

options.text: The Edge Runtime is deprecated for route segments; remove the export
options.why: The segment config reference marks `'edge'` deprecated, with `'nodejs'` the default.

options.text: Cache Components doesn't support it; edge logic belongs in Proxy
options.why: The migration guide says to switch to Node.js and use Proxy for edge behaviour.

options.text: It is still the default runtime for pages that stream with Suspense
options.why: The default is `'nodejs'`, and streaming works there.

options.text: It is required for time-based ISR with a `revalidate` export
options.why: The opposite: `revalidate` is not available on the edge runtime.

options.text: It unlocks extra segment config such as `revalidate` and `fetchCache`
options.why: Those options are not available on edge; they are a Node.js-runtime feature.

explanation: In Next.js 16 the `runtime` segment option defaults to `'nodejs'`, and `'edge'` is deprecated. Cache Components requires the Node.js runtime, so routes exporting `runtime = 'edge'` must drop it. For edge-style request logic, the docs point to Proxy.

stem: An app enables `cacheComponents` and `partialPrefetching`. `app/[category]/layout.tsx` lists the categories `tops` and `shorts` in `generateStaticParams`, and `app/[category]/[product]/page.tsx` lists one product per category (`tee`, `joggers`). Both read params inside `<Suspense>`. What does the first visitor to `/tops/overshirt` get, and later visitors?

options.text: The tops App Shell with the product streaming; later visits get the cached upgrade
options.why: Known params fill in, unknown ones stream, and the result is cached after the first visit.

options.text: A 404 page, because `overshirt` was not returned by the page's generateStaticParams
options.why: Cache Components renders unlisted params on request; a 404 needs an explicit notFound().

options.text: A full request-time render on every visit, because unlisted products are never cached
options.why: After the first visit, the upgraded page is cached for later visitors.

options.text: The generic `/[category]/[product]` App Shell, with both header and product streaming every time
options.why: The tops category was prerendered, so its header is already in the shell.

explanation: At build time Next.js prerenders `/tops/tee`, `/shorts/joggers`, the App Shells `/tops/[product]` and `/shorts/[product]`, and the generic `/[category]/[product]`. A first visit to an unlisted product under a known category gets that category's App Shell instantly, then the page is upgraded in the background and later visits skip the shell. This is the Cache Components version of ISR.
reference: Next.js docs: ISR with Cache Components

stem: In the app from the previous question, the category layout passes `params` into a `<Suspense>`-wrapped header instead of awaiting it, even for categories that `generateStaticParams` lists. Why do the docs recommend this?

options.text: Awaiting a known param above it would tie the layout's App Shell to one URL
options.why: The URL-independent shell is what unknown categories and navigations reuse.

options.text: Known params resolve faster inside Suspense, so the static shell paints sooner
options.why: Speed is not the reason; it is about keeping the shell reusable.

options.text: generateStaticParams is ignored for any params awaited outside a Suspense boundary
options.why: The listed params are still prerendered either way.

options.text: Awaiting params outside Suspense would turn the layout into a Client Component
options.why: Awaiting never changes a component's server or client nature.

explanation: The ISR guide says to keep the read inside the boundary even for covered categories: a statically known param still belongs to one URL, and awaiting it above the boundary would tie the layout's App Shell to that URL. Reading it inside `<Suspense>` keeps a generic shell that works for unknown params and instant navigations.
reference: Next.js docs: ISR with Cache Components (Prepare your routes)

stem:
With Cache Components, a page reads a config file that never changes between deploys:

```tsx
import { readFile } from 'node:fs/promises'

export default async function Page() {
  const items = JSON.parse(await readFile('./config.json', 'utf-8')).items
  return <List items={items} />
}
```

What happens, and what is the simplest fix?

options.text: It counts as uncached data; read the file once at module scope instead
options.why: A file that never changes can be read at module load, outside rendering.

options.text: It completes during prerendering like readFileSync, so nothing needs to change
options.why: Only synchronous reads complete automatically; an awaited read counts as uncached.

options.text: It throws, because node:fs is not available in Server Components
options.why: Server Components run in Node.js and can use the file system.

options.text: It works in development but goes stale, so add `export const revalidate = 0`
options.why: `revalidate` is a previous-model option and is removed under Cache Components.

explanation: Under Cache Components, an awaited `readFile()` during rendering is treated like any uncached data: it must be inside `'use cache'` or behind `<Suspense>`. Module imports, `fs.readFileSync` and pure computations complete during prerender. For a file that is the same on every request, the docs recommend reading it once at module scope (top-level await).

stem: With Cache Components, a footer shows a visitor count read with `better-sqlite3`, a synchronous driver. In production the number never changes from its value at build time. Why, and what fixes it?

options.text: Sync queries finish during prerender; call await connection() first, inside Suspense
options.why: That stops prerendering before the query, so it runs per request.

options.text: SQLite results are deduplicated like fetch calls; pass `cache: 'no-store'` to the query
options.why: better-sqlite3 has no fetch cache options; the issue is prerendering.

options.text: The count is held in the client router cache, so call `router.refresh()` on mount
options.why: The stale value is baked into the prerendered HTML, not the client cache.

options.text: better-sqlite3 only runs at build time, so move the query into a Route Handler
options.why: It runs fine at request time once prerendering is stopped before it.

explanation: Queries from synchronous drivers such as `better-sqlite3` or `node:sqlite` complete during prerendering, so their result ends up in the static shell. The docs say to call `await connection()` before the query, inside a `<Suspense>` boundary, to exclude it from prerendering when you need per-request data.

stem:
With Cache Components, a page renders a static `

` and nav, a `` component that uses `'use cache'` with `cacheLife('hours')`, and `Loading your preferences...

}>`, where `Prefs` reads `cookies()`. Another `` wraps ``, which runs an uncached `fetch`. Which three end up in the prerendered static shell? (Choose three.)

options.text: The `<h1>` and the navigation links
options.why: Static markup is always prerendered.

options.text: The rendered output of `<Posts />`
options.why: Cached results with a long enough lifetime join the shell.

options.text: The text "Loading your preferences..."
options.why: Suspense fallbacks ship with the shell.

options.text: The theme that `<Prefs />` reads from the cookie
options.why: Cookie-dependent content streams at request time.

options.text: The articles returned by `<Latest />`'s uncached fetch
options.why: Uncached data streams behind its fallback.

options.text: Per-user content derived from `headers()`
options.why: Headers are a runtime API, so this also streams later.

explanation: During prerendering, static content, `'use cache'` results (with a lifetime that is not too short) and Suspense fallbacks form the static shell. Content that needs runtime APIs or uncached data streams in at request time behind its fallback. That is the static, cached and streaming mix the caching docs describe.
reference: Next.js docs: Caching (Static, cached, and streaming)

stem: Working without Cache Components, a page exports `revalidate = 0` and makes two requests: `fetch(a)` with no cache option and `fetch(b, { cache: 'force-cache' })`. What happens?

options.text: It renders per request; fetch(a) is uncached while fetch(b) stays cached
options.why: `revalidate = 0` only changes the default for fetches that set no cache option.

options.text: Both fetches go to the network on every request, since revalidate = 0 overrides force-cache
options.why: Fetches that opt into force-cache keep their behaviour.

options.text: The page is static, because force-cache makes the whole route cacheable
options.why: `revalidate = 0` guarantees the page renders dynamically.

options.text: The build fails, because the segment config and the fetch options conflict
options.why: Mixing them is allowed; there is no conflict error.

explanation: Per the segment config docs, `revalidate = 0` makes the layout or page always render dynamically and changes the default of fetches without a `cache` option to `no-store`. It leaves fetches that opt into `force-cache` or use a positive `revalidate` unchanged. To force every fetch to the network, use `fetchCache = 'force-no-store'` or `dynamic = 'force-dynamic'`.
